title: Architecture standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Amelia Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and standards across API, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is the canonical reference for engineers and system owners implementing or operating platform components. Where specific, concrete thresholds or command examples are provided, follow them unless a documented exception exists and is approved via an ADR.

Goals
- Provide a consistent, developer-friendly API surface and versioning policy.
- Ensure predictable, secure infrastructure and deployments (hosted, dedicated, private).
- Standardize model-serving practices to meet latency, cost, and reliability targets.
- Define observability and performance requirements to detect regressions early.
- Document decision records and approval flows to maintain architectural clarity.

1. API Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent, discoverable, and stable APIs for external and internal consumers.

Core principles:
- Resource-based design for REST endpoints; prefer RPC for internal high-throughput paths only.
- Semantic versioning in the URL and headers: include minor/major versions for breaking changes.
- Strong contract-first approach: OpenAPI v3 for public endpoints, with a canonical spec in the docs repo.

Naming and versioning:
- Endpoint pattern: /v{major}/{resource}/{action} (e.g., /v1/models/generate).
- Release policy: Major version bump for breaking changes, minor/patch for backwards-compatible changes.
- Deprecation: Announce 30 days before minor removals, 90 days for breaking changes affecting customers.

Errors and rate limits:
- Use standard HTTP status codes. Body must include: {"error": "short_key", "message": "human readable", "details": null}.
- Rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset).
- Error budget policy detailed in eng-sre/runbooks; recoverable server errors (5xx) should be <0.1% per hour per-route.

Example OpenAPI fragment (public endpoints):
- See /repos/docs/api/openapi/models.yaml

CLI and SDK calls (examples):
- curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/models/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"model":"redwood-text-2","prompt":"Hello"}'

Backward compatibility checklist for API changes:
1. Additive-only schema changes first (new optional fields).
2. Add feature flag behind a per-route toggle and enable for internal traffic.
3. Canary rollout, see rollout steps below.

2. Coding Standards
Purpose: Maintain code quality, readability, and consistency across services.

Languages and layering:
- Runtime services: Go (1.21+) for low-latency components.
- Model orchestration and tooling: Rust and Go where performance-critical; Python for evals/experiments and SDKs.
- SDKs: TypeScript/Node, Python, and Java maintained in the SDK monorepo.

Linting and CI:
- Enforce golangci-lint for Go, ruff/black/isort for Python, eslint/prettier for TypeScript.
- CI gating: all PRs require unit tests and a successful build.
- Test coverage target: >= 85% for core infra packages; >= 70% for peripheral services.

Repository layout and dependency rules:
- Use small, single-responsibility services. Keep public API surface minimal.
- Dependabot for automated dependency updates; security patches applied within 48 hours.
- Use pinned Terraform module versions in infra repos.

Coding conventions (examples):
- Error handling: prefer explicit error returns and wrapping (Go) over panics.
- Context propagation: accept context.Context for all RPC/handler signatures.
- Secrets: never commit secrets to repo; use Vault/KMS integrations.

3. Infrastructure Standards
Purpose: Secure, reproducible, and auditable infrastructure deployments.

IaC and state:
- Terraform is the canonical IaC tool. Modules must be published to the shared-module registry and reused.
- Remote state: S3 with encryption, DynamoDB locking; state buckets named rdinfr-state-<env>.

Networking and isolation:
- VPC per environment; zero-trust by default. Private deployments get isolated VPCs and optional customer-managed networks.
- Subnet and routing conventions are documented in eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures.

Identity and secrets:
- Use IAM roles for services and short-lived credentials.
- KMS keys per-customer for Private deployments; keys rotated annually.

Terraform example (snippet):
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "tf_state" {
  bucket = "rdinfr-state-prod"
  server_side_encryption_configuration {
    rule {
      apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
        sse_algorithm = "aws:kms"
        kms_master_key_id = var.kms_key_id
      }
    }
  }
}

Deployment and rollout policy:
- CI -> canary -> gradual rollout -> full. See rollout checklist below.

4. Model-Serving Standards
Purpose: Ensure models are served with predictable latency, cost, and correctness.

Model artifacts and manifest:
- Every model must include a model-manifest.json with: model_id, version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, recommended_batch_sizes, validated_seq_lengths, and owner.
- Store manifests and artifacts in the model registry bucket: s3://rdinfr-models/<model_id>/<version>/.

Versioning and compatibility:
- Semantic model versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Backwards-incompatible tokenizer or architecture changes require MAJOR bump.
- Runtime compatibility matrix maintained in eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture.

Quantization and profiles:
- Approved quantization profiles live under confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles.
- When shipping a quantized variant, include evaluation artifacts showing quality regression < 2% (task-dependent).

Autoscaling and batching:
- Autoscaler triggers: CPU/GPU utilization > 70% sustained for 60s OR queue length > recommended_batch_size * 2 for 30s.
- Default batch sizing policy: continuous batching with dynamic batch caps based on sequence-length distribution.
- Example policy: if median_seq_len < 128 -> max_batch 64; if median_seq_len 128-512 -> max_batch 32; else max_batch 8.

Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
- Model variants: full-precision -> quantized -> distilled. Router policy should prefer lower-latency variant within same quality band and fallback on errors.
- Circuit breaker: 5xx rate > 1% over 5m triggers automatic fallback to previous stable model.

Operational runbooks:
- See eng-serving-runtime/runbooks for troubleshooting: high-latency, KV cache corruption, OOM in GPU containers.

5. Observability Standards
Purpose: Provide complete telemetry to diagnose performance, reliability, and cost anomalies.

Metrics (Prometheus naming conventions):
- request_latency_seconds{route,model_id} (histogram). SLO example: p50 < 50ms, p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms for control-plane endpoints; model generation endpoints have route-specific SLOs documented in runbooks.
- tokens_generated_total{model_id,customer_id} (counter).
- model_gpu_utilization_percent{host,model_id} (gauge).
- error_rate_total{route,code} (counter).

Traces and logs:
- Use OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing. Required spans: api.request, runtime.infer, kvcache.lookup, model.kernel_exec.
- Sampling: default 1% for production; 100% for traces containing errors or sampling flag.
- Logs must be structured JSON, include trace_id, span_id, request_id, model_id, customer_id (when permitted), and severity.

Dashboards and alerts:
- Dashboards per route/model: latency heatmap, throughput, error rate, cost per token.
- Alerting thresholds: page on sustained p99 latency breach > 2x SLO for 10m, or error rate > 1% for 5m.

6. Performance Standards and Benchmarking
Purpose: Maintain predictable unit economics and regression detection.

Benchmarking harness:
- Use the canonical benchmarking suite under eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks must run weekly on representative hardware (A100 40GB, H100 where available).
- Store benchmark artifacts and golden traces for regression comparison.

Example performance table (guideline):
| model | seq_len | batch | tokens/sec | target p95 latency | GPU |
| redwood-text-2-1.0 | 128 | 32 | 1200 | < 150ms | A100-40GB |
| redwood-chat-1.0 | 512 | 8 | 450 | < 300ms | A100-80GB |
| open-llama-3 | 256 | 16 | 900 | < 200ms | H100 |

Regression policy:
- Any benchmark regression > 5% tokens/sec or > 10% p95 latency must open a regression triage ticket in applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage and notify the model-onboarding owner.

7. ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
Purpose: Ensure architectural decisions are documented, discoverable, and reversible.

ADR template (default fields):
- ADR ID: YYYY-NNN (year and sequence)
- Title
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded
- Context
- Decision
- Consequences
- Owners and reviewers
- Related ADRs / linked pages

Process:
1. Draft ADR and add to confluence under architecture-and-standards/decision-records with the ADR ID in the filename.
2. Assign reviewers (minimum one arch lead and one service owner).
3. Review window: 5 business days for non-breaking/platform changes; 10 business days for breaking platform changes.
4. Approval: sign-off by owner_team lead and architecture guild representative.
5. If approved, update status to accepted and add to the ADR index.

Example ADR that changed default batch policy:
- ADR-2026-002: Dynamic batching caps based on median sequence length. See eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture for implementation notes.

8. Rollout and Canary Checklist (applies across infra, runtime, and API changes)
1. Create feature flag for change where possible.
2. Internal canary (10% internal traffic) for 1 hour; monitor latency, error rate, cost.
3. Externally visible canary (1% production traffic) for 30 minutes; automatic rollback if error_rate > 0.5% OR p95 latency exceeds 2x SLO.
4. Gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with at least 30 minutes observed at each stage and green health checks.
5. Post-rollout: schedule a 24h review in the deployment runbook; confirm metrics meet expectations.

Contacts and ownership
- Architecture guild: architecture@redwood.ai
- Eng serving runtime: eng-serving-runtime@redwood.ai (owner for model-serving standards)
- Platform & infra: eng-infra@redwood.ai
- Observability: eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts team alias

Appendices
A. Exceptions and change requests
- To deviate from any standard open an ADR with rationale and mitigation steps. Emergency exceptions must be recorded within 48h of change.

B. Quick reference commands
- Terraform plan: terraform -chdir=infra/prod plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
- Apply with locking: terraform -chdir=infra/prod apply -var-file=prod.tfvars
- Run benchmark: ./perf/run_benchmark.sh --model redwood-text-2 --seq 128 --batch 32 --out artifacts/redwood-text-2-2026-03-01.json

C. Example model-manifest.json (compact)
{
  "model_id": "redwood-text-2",
  "version": "1.0.2",
  "architecture": "transformer-decoder",
  "tokenizer": "bpe-v2",
  "quantization_profile": "q4_0",
  "recommended_batch_sizes": "[8,16,32]",
  "validated_seq_lengths": "[128,256,512]",
  "owner": "eng-serving-runtime"
}

D. Useful links
- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (internal)
- applied-ml-and-evals/benchmarking-and-perf-suite (internal)
- confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records (ADR index)

Owners

For questions or to request an exception, open a ticket in the architecture board and tag architecture@redwood.ai.
